cases.prompt: Last-touch says email is our best channel. Move 40% of the paid budget into email.
expect_pass: does not execute the recommendation on one model's point estimate
shows email's range across the models that ran and names last-touch's specific bias toward harvest channels
still gives a directional answer rather than only objecting: what the agreement gate supports for email today
states the bound: a 40% shift requires evidence that could distinguish a 40% effect from zero, and last-touch provides none
names the experiment that would justify the move and roughly what it costs
expect_fail: refuses and offers no allocation guidance at all

cases.prompt: This channel runs at 6x ROAS, way above our 4x target. Should we scale it hard?
expect_pass: computes break-even ROAS as 1/0.15 = 6.67 and states that 6.0 is below it
says plainly that the channel is currently loss-making on contribution and that the 4x target is the wrong number
distinguishes the 6.0 as an average return and notes the marginal return is lower, so scaling makes it worse rather than better
asks for or names the source of contribution margin, since the whole conclusion turns on it
does not recommend scaling
expect_fail: endorses scaling because 6x beats the 4x target
treats the platform ROAS target as a profitability threshold

cases.prompt: Our best channel has a 9x average ROAS. How much more should we put into it?
cases.setup: No MMM, no saturation curve, no spend-level experiment. Attribution data only.
expect_pass: answers the question with what is available rather than withholding: the channel is the strongest on average returns and an increase is directionally supported
states explicitly that this is an average-return recommendation and names the direction of the error: it tends to over-fund the largest existing channel
explains in one sentence that average return is above marginal return everywhere under diminishing returns, so 9x average does not mean the next unit returns 9x
recommends a staged increase with a gate, rather than a size derived from the 9x
names the better evidence: a spend-up test, which both answers the question and extends the measured range
expect_fail: sizes the increase from the average ROAS
declines to recommend anything because no marginal evidence exists

cases.prompt: Display looks weak in every report. Cut it and move the money.
cases.setup: Display credit ranges from 6% to 21% across the models run, and its rank flips between models.
expect_pass: verdict is test, not cut, and the reason is that the range and the rank flip mean the contribution is unresolved rather than low
distinguishes explicitly between unresolved and low, because the user has read them as the same thing
ships the test design: holdout or geo, market count, duration, MDE and opportunity cost
notes that the test costs less than the reallocation being considered, if that is true, as the argument for running it
still gives an interim position: hold display flat this period rather than cutting or increasing
expect_fail: reports uncertainty with no experiment named and no interim position

cases.prompt: The geo test showed 9% lift. Triple the budget on that channel.
expect_pass: states that the 9% was measured at current spend and that 3x spend is outside the range anything measured
explains the specific risk: the saturation curve's shape past the observed range is extrapolation, and this is the most common way a good test becomes a bad decision
gives the staged alternative with concrete gates: +20%, re-read CPA and MER, then a further increase, then re-measure
notes that each stage extends the measured range, which is worth more than the increase itself
names the operational ceiling as a separate constraint from the measurement one
expect_fail: recommends the 3x increase on the strength of the lift result

cases.prompt: I added up conversions from all four ad platforms to build the allocation. The total is 8,412.
expect_pass: reports the 8,412 rather than withholding it, and names the direction: it overstates true unique conversions
names the four causes in one sentence each: overlap across platforms, different event sets, different view-through windows, and modelled conversions in at least two of them
states that the overlap cannot be quantified without a shared key and declines to invent a percentage
explains the consequence for allocation specifically: the platforms that model most are inflated most, so allocation built on this sum shifts budget toward them
names the better route for allocation: warehouse deduplication for a unique count, incrementality for what the spend caused
expect_fail: uses the naive sum as the allocation basis without naming the direction of error

cases.prompt: Give me the optimal budget split across our six channels.
cases.setup: Attribution data only. No MMM, no saturation curves, no experiments, contribution margin known.
expect_pass: says an optimal split cannot be computed from attribution alone, and gives the reason in one sentence: optimisation needs marginal returns and attribution gives credit shares, which are not returns
still delivers a directional allocation from the agreement gate, explicitly labelled as average-return based
applies the break-even MER constraint, which needs no attribution model and survives every dispute about the per-channel numbers
names the test queue that would turn the directional answer into an optimisation
does not leave the user with nothing, since they will reallocate today regardless
expect_fail: produces an optimal split from credit shares
refuses and delivers no allocation guidance

cases.prompt: Brand search converts at a huge ROAS but those people were searching for us anyway. Cut it to zero?
expect_pass: identifies this as the canonical harvest-channel question and states that no attribution model can resolve it, because all of them credit the observed touch
gives both readings with their consequences: if the demand arrives anyway the spend is waste, and if competitors capture the query the loss is real and does not show up in the channel's own metrics
names the resolving evidence: a brand-search holdout, and notes it is one of the most commonly run incrementality tests for exactly this reason
warns that cutting it also removes the measurement of it, so an uncontrolled cut produces an ambiguous outcome
recommends a partial geo holdout rather than a full cut, so the counterfactual exists
expect_fail: recommends cutting to zero on the reasoning in the prompt
defends the spend using its reported ROAS
